title: A droplet bouncing on a shaking bath walks along by surfing its own ripples

cover.alt: A dark, shiny droplet sitting on a smooth greenish liquid surface, with faint ripples around it.

body: Shake a bath of silicone oil up and down and a droplet of the same oil can bounce on it instead of merging, because a thin layer of air stays trapped beneath it. Each bounce sends out ripples, and with the right shaking the droplet is pushed along by its own waves, so it **walks** across the surface. Ordinary walkers are about 1 mm across and move at about 1 cm a second. [In 2019, researchers in Australia](https://phys.org/news/2019-07-droplets-liquid-surface.html) found that shaking the bath at two frequencies at once makes bigger, faster 'superwalkers', like the one filmed here.

slides.alt: Close-up high-speed footage of a dark droplet bouncing again and again on a greenish liquid surface. Rings of ripples spread from it, and its reflection appears below it at each impact, as it drifts steadily to the right.
slides.caption: High-speed footage of a superwalker: the droplet bounces on a vibrating bath of the same liquid, sending out ripples as it travels across the surface.
slides.music: “Myst on the Moor” Kevin MacLeod (incompetech.com) · CC BY 4.0

slides.prompt: The droplet is made of the same oil as the bath. Why doesn't it simply merge into it?
slides.detail: Each time it lands, a layer of air is trapped beneath it, and the bath's shaking launches it again before the air can drain away.

left.label: Walker
left.text: Bath shaken at one frequency, such as 80 Hz. About 1 mm across, moving at about 1 cm a second.

right.label: Superwalker
right.text: Bath shaken at 80 Hz and 40 Hz together. Up to 2.8 mm across, moving at about 5 cm a second.

slides.heading: Fact or myth?

items.text: Walkers can cross barriers, less often as they widen
Pairs of walkers orbit at set distances
Every team has seen double-slit interference

slides.explanation: Walkers are entirely classical, yet mimic tunnelling and quantised orbits. In 2015, three teams found no double-slit interference.

slides.heading: Quantum lookalikes
slides.text: Yves Couder's lab was the first to study walkers systematically, in 2005. They have since become a tabletop analogy for some quantum systems, though it has limits: their paths are easily disturbed by the container's walls and by air currents.
